Lead story

Ray: Okay, so the problem. Near a phase transition, physicists expect clean power laws, and the exponents in them tell you about universal behavior. But the authors point out that weak first order transitions can fake this. They can show a long stretch of what's called pseudocritical scaling, which mimics the real thing.

Ada: So which system are we talking about?

Ray: The dilute Baxter Wu model, a spin model whose apparent criticality has been debated for a long time. The paper says that behavior comes from a marginally relevant renormalization group flow. Renormalization group is the math of how a system's couplings change as you zoom out. Marginally relevant means a coupling creeps along very slowly, but eventually it wins, and drives the system into a first order regime with phase coexistence.

Ada: Right. So how did they show it? What did they actually do?

Ray: Two tools together. Conformal perturbation theory, which starts from a critical point and nudges it. And tensor network level spectroscopy, resolved by symmetry, which reads off energy levels from a tensor network calculation, sorted by their symmetries. With those, they wrote a slowly running coupling in a form you can compute numerically, and built a flow based diagnostic from it.

Ada: Is that an experiment, or a calculation?

Ray: A calculation. The abstract describes theory and numerics, not a lab measurement.

Ada: And does the diagnostic work beyond this one model? They call it generic.

Ray: The abstract calls it generic, but it only describes applying it to the Baxter Wu models. It doesn't say how it fares elsewhere. What it does report is that the flows of the dilute and self dual Baxter Wu models collapse onto the multicritical phase diagram of the dilute four state Potts model, which shows the flow on both sides of the Potts point.

Ada: Okay, but why should anyone outside this corner care?

Ray: Here's the thing. If you fit critical exponents from finite size data, a clean power law can fool you. This gives a way to ask whether the coupling is still quietly running.

Magnets and materials

Ray: On to magnets and materials. First, a symmetry paper from Sang Wook Cheong, Lei Han, and Fei Ting Huang in Physical Review Materials.

Ada: Kinetomagnetism. Say what that is.

Ray: Magnetization, or related responses, induced by linear momentum or equivalent stimuli. The abstract says the necessary and sufficient condition is broken parity time symmetry. And all altermagnets can show it. Some types support even order responses, another type supports odd order ones.

Ada: So, a classification, not a prediction for a specific material.

Ray: Exactly. It's a framework. It ties together piezomagnetism, higher order nonlinear Hall responses, and spin splitting torques.

Ray: Next, cerium. Angle resolved photoemission on the compound cerium silver bismuth two, plus resonant photoemission and first principles calculations.

Ada: Is it a magnet?

Ray: No, it's a Kondo lattice. They resolve a nearly flat cerium four f band near the Fermi level, and momentum dependent mixing between those f electrons and Dirac derived bands. Their reading is that the Dirac band connectivity survives the heavy quasiparticle renormalization.

Ray: And a title only item. A physics guided convolutional neural network that infers the Dzyaloshinskii Moriya interaction and disorder from magnetic domain images.

Ada: Title only means no numbers, no accuracy. I'd want to know how much training data it needs.

Ray: The story doesn't say. Unconfirmed.

Weird physics corner

Ray: Weird physics corner. Imagine a lithographic array of tiny nanomagnets, called artificial spin ice, in a square kagome arrangement.

Ada: Square kagome. Sounds like a yoga pose.

Ray: Ha! In the spin foam phase, relaxation follows Boltzmann statistics. But in the spin crystal phase, domain walls get trapped in non Boltzmann distributions, even though energetically better routes exist. The ordered background lacks the facilitators needed to connect different classes of domain walls.

Ada: So the system gets stuck because it lacks the moves.

Ray: Yes. Experiment and Monte Carlo simulation both show it. Kinetics overrides energetics.

Ray: And a Nature Physics study demonstrated the Aharonov Bohm effect in a lattice gauge theory simulation on a hybrid trapped ion quantum computer. That effect is a quantum phase from enclosed magnetic flux. The summary gives little more.

Dilute Baxter–Wu 'criticality' is a marginal flow to first order

arXiv · spin models & criticality · 8/10

The abstract reports that apparent criticality in the dilute Baxter–Wu model comes from a marginally relevant renormalization-group flow that ends in first-order coexistence, not a true critical point. The authors use conformal perturbation theory and tensor-network level spectroscopy to build a flow-based diagnostic. The broader lesson is that a clean-looking power law near a transition can be pseudocritical, which matters for anyone fitting critical exponents from finite-size data.

Kinetomagnetism unified with altermagnetism through symmetry classification

Physical Review Materials · 8/10

The abstract reports that broken combined parity-time (PT) symmetry is both necessary and sufficient for kinetomagnetism, and that all altermagnets can show it. It says the framework unifies piezomagnetism, nonlinear Hall responses and spin-splitting torques under one symmetry classification. It is a symmetry framework rather than a quantitative calculation of any specific material's anisotropy.

ARPES shows Kondo hybridization of Dirac-derived bands in CeAgBi2

arXiv · spin models & criticality · 6/10

The abstract reports ARPES measurements, Ce 4d→4f resonant photoemission and first-principles calculations on CeAgBi2. Together they resolve a nearly dispersionless 4f band near the Fermi level and momentum-dependent hybridization between the cerium f-electrons and Dirac-derived bands. It is a Kondo lattice rather than a magnet, but it shows how localized cerium f-states mix with conduction electrons.

TmZnGaO4 triangular antiferromagnet shows easy-c-axis anisotropy and a 1/3 plateau

Physical Review Materials · 7/10

The abstract reports single crystals with strong easy-c-axis anisotropy from magnetization curves and a one-third magnetization plateau consistent with up-up-down order. Specific heat shows broad anomalies at 0.11 K and 2.81 K rather than a sharp long-range ordering transition. It is a clean directional test case for Ising-like behavior in a non-Kramers rare-earth antiferromagnet, not a ferromagnet.

Phase3D launches custom LPBF Fringe Inspection hardware

3D Printing Industry · 5/10

The item states that Phase3D's new generation of its Fringe Inspection platform uses purpose-built hardware for integration into laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) metal printers, replacing off-the-shelf components. The summary includes no validation data, so claims about defect detection remain unconfirmed. It reflects a broader trend of inspection sensing moving from add-on equipment into the printer itself.

ML · Magnetic Materials

Physics-guided CNN infers DMI and disorder from domain images

J. Magnetism & Magnetic Materials · 6/10

Only the title is available, so details are unconfirmed. The title suggests a convolutional neural network guided by physics to extract magnetic parameters, such as the Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya interaction (DMI) and disorder, from images of magnetic domains. If it works with limited data, it could speed up imaging-based magnetic characterization.

Genetic algorithm designs interpretable spatial descriptors with SHAP attribution

arXiv · ML materials discovery · 6/10

The abstract reports a genetic algorithm that searches over spatial partitions and pooling operations, balancing prediction error against the number of descriptors. It says the approach extends to molecules and solids. The demonstrations appear to involve microscopy spectra and hysteresis loops, so its use on crystal structures is untested in the summary.

Spin reorientation in CrSBr shifts a light–matter condensate by over 10 meV

Nature Materials · 5/10

The summary reports that reorienting the spins with a modest magnetic field shifts the color of a light–matter condensate in layered CrSBr by more than 10 meV. It shows how directly magnetic anisotropy can couple to an optical readout. It is photonics work, and the summary gives few details.

Quantum Monte Carlo finds positronium-like bound states in quantum spin ice

arXiv · magnetism + ML · 6/10

The abstract reports quantum Monte Carlo with stochastic analytic continuation at the Rokhsar–Kivelson point, revealing a double-peaked electric-monopole spectrum. The lower peak is attributed to a bound pair of monopoles, a positronium-like state. It is a methods-focused result on simulating quantum spin systems.

Additive Manufacturing

Particle inertia and large-pore formation in powder-blown DED

J. Manufacturing Processes · 5/10

Only the title is available, so details are unconfirmed. It links particle inertia to large-pore formation and to material-dependent melt-pool response in directed energy deposition (DED), where powder is blown into a melt. If the link holds, it is a process–defect connection that could inform in-process monitoring. It concerns DED rather than laser powder bed fusion.

EvSLAM benchmark tests event cameras under aggressive 6-DoF motion

arXiv · event-based vision · 6/10

The abstract reports an analysis of state-of-the-art event-based visual odometry and a new benchmark spanning varied platforms, extreme lighting and aggressive six-degree-of-freedom motion. Event cameras report per-pixel brightness changes instead of full frames, which makes them fast and robust in hard conditions. It is a robotics evaluation rather than melt-pool sensing, but it shows how event-camera methods are being stress-tested.

IMI qualifies AM nickel-alloy valve parts to DNV-ST-B203 Level 3

Additive Manufacturing Media · 5/10

The item states that IMI and TotalEnergies EP Denmark qualified additively manufactured disk stacks for hydrogen-sulphide service at AMC Level 3 under DNV-ST-B203. Qualifying printed valve parts for sour service is a concrete step toward safety-critical industrial use. The item does not say whether in-situ monitoring was part of the qualification evidence.

Snowbird reports savings from DED parts printed during RIMPAC 2026

TCT Magazine · 5/10

The item states that Snowbird's deployable hybrid system, using Meltio DED printing, produced parts aboard the USS Essex and ashore during the RIMPAC 2026 naval exercise. It is a field data point for defense use of additive manufacturing. The cost-savings claims are summarized without supporting data.

Theoretical Physics

Artificial spin ice shows kinetics overriding energetics, checked by Monte Carlo

arXiv · statistical mechanics · 6/10

The abstract reports that in a square-kagome nanomagnet array, the spin-foam phase relaxes with Boltzmann statistics, while the spin-crystal phase traps domain walls in non-Boltzmann distributions. Experiments and Monte Carlo simulations both show this. In plain terms, the system can get stuck short of its lowest-energy states because it lacks the moves needed to reach them.

Functional RG gets Yang–Lee edge exponents across dimensions

arXiv · high-energy theory · 6/10

The abstract reports fourth-order derivative-expansion functional renormalization-group results, such as η = -0.575(9) in three dimensions, that agree with six-loop epsilon-expansion calculations. It also traces earlier hyperscaling violations to the neglected motion of the expansion point. The Yang–Lee edge is where a magnet's partition function in an imaginary field first becomes singular, making it a stringent benchmark for computing universal exponents.

Trapped ions simulate Aharonov–Bohm interference in a lattice gauge theory

Phys.org · Quantum physics · 6/10

The summary says a Nature Physics study demonstrated the Aharonov–Bohm effect in a quantum simulation of a lattice gauge theory on a hybrid trapped-ion computer. The effect is a quantum phase a charge picks up from enclosed magnetic flux even where it feels no force. Here the simulator reproduces that behavior inside a gauge theory. Details beyond the summary are unconfirmed.

Diffusion generators decide spin-glass structure in a fixed order

arXiv · statistical mechanics · 6/10

The abstract reports that path-integral diffusion samplers are equivalent to time-changed Gaussian stochastic localization, so what gets decided does not depend on the protocol, only on when decisions occur and at what cost. On Sherrington–Kirkpatrick and Bethe spin glasses of up to 64 spins, a trajectory first picks one of two mirror-image halves, then the glassy classes within it. This links generative machine learning to the structure of spin glasses.
